==Problem 17==
Four students are seated in a row. They chat with the people sitting next to them, then rearrange themselves so that they are no longer seated next to any of the same people. How many rearrangements are possible?

[[File:2026 amc 8 q17.png | 650px]]

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 2 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 4 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 9 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 12 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 24</imath>

==Solution 1 (AMC 10 Bijection)==

Label the human beings A, B, C, and D in that order from left to right. It doesn't matter the original configuration. Now, the problem is:

How many four letter strings ABCD exist such that A is not next to B, B not next to C, and C is not next to D.

We can count the number of strings manually (or just do casework), to obtain <imath>\boxed{2}</imath>.

This is incredibly similar to one AMC 10 problem, that asked how many four letter strings abcd have no two consecutive letters in the alphabet next to one another.

~Pinotation

==Solution 2==
Let's say the people are <imath>A</imath>, <imath>B</imath>, <imath>C</imath>, and <imath>D</imath>, and they seated in the order <imath>ABCD</imath> at first. <imath>A</imath> cannot be next to <imath>B</imath>, <imath>B</imath> cannot be next to <imath>C</imath>, and <imath>C</imath> cannot be next to <imath>D</imath>, so our only possibilities are <imath>CADB</imath> and <imath>BDAC</imath> as orders, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\mathbf{(A) 2}}</imath>.

~Yuhao2012

==Solution 3==
Since <imath>B</imath> sits next to both <imath>A</imath> and <imath>C</imath>, <imath>B</imath> can only sit next to <imath>D</imath>. The only way this is possible is if <imath>B</imath> sits at either the front or the back. We can apply this same logic to <imath>C.</imath> There are now two cases: <imath>BDAC</imath> or <imath>CADB,</imath> which is the former with its order reversed. Therefore, our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf {(A)} 2}</imath>.

~clever14710owl
